title: Danish Pastries and Croissant
summary: ## Rich yeast doughs and enriching agents

Yeast doughs can be enriched by using eggs, butter etc. to take on cake like qualities. Eggs make the bread lighter and more moist and butter gives it a tender, almost melting texture. Egg and butter are the commonly used enriching agents. Most of these enriched rolls are traditionally eaten at breakfast time.

Brioche is the richest of all yeast breads as it contains a lot of butter and eggs; it requires a longer time for fermentation and proving, which improves its flavour and silky texture. It is best eaten warm and fresh, and with its moistness and high fat content it keeps for several days. The dough can be made in advance and stored for a day or two in the refrigerator. It is made in three parts: a starter dough (yeast dissolved in lukewarm milk and a little flour), a second dough and then both are kneaded together. A starter dough is a small, soft, smooth dough of yeast, milk and flour which is kept covered in a warm place for about 30 minutes before mixing it into the rest of the dough. Doughnuts are one of the rare bakery items which are not baked but deep fried; a raising agent, either yeast or baking powder, is used. New oil should be used for frying so that they do not take on unwanted flavours. The dough is rolled to 1/2 inch, cut with a doughnut cutter, proved on a floured duster, fried until golden brown, drained and rolled in cinnamon sugar.

Croissants (crescent rolls) are the favourites on a French breakfast table. They are prepared from a lightly enriched yeast dough interleaved with thin layers of butter, called a leavened puff dough: leavened as yeast has been used for raising and puff because butter is added in the same manner as for flaky pastry. The dough is raised both by yeast and by the butter's moisture, which turns to steam during baking and separates the layers into light flakes. Fat is added in three lots of 50 g; the dough is not rolled with too much pressure so that fat does not come out; a book fold is given at the end; it is rolled to 1/8 inch, cut into triangles, rolled up from the base into a crescent, proved for 35-45 minutes, egg washed and baked at 200 C for 15-20 minutes. Danish pastry is a yeast puff dough cut into various shapes (envelopes, pinwheels, cockscombs) and folded around sweet or savoury fillings; these are known as coffee or breakfast breads. They are baked at 200 C for 20 minutes, brushed with apricot jam sauce and decorated with fondant icing.

sa: What is a starter dough? Why is it prepared?

(i) A starter dough is a small soft dough made by dissolving yeast in lukewarm milk and adding a little flour. (ii) It is kept covered in a warm place for about 30 minutes until it doubles in volume. (iii) It is then mixed into the rest of the dough. (iv) It makes the yeast active and gives richer doughs like brioche and croissant a good rise, flavour and texture. (v) Such doughs need a long, unhurried fermentation.
Describe the method of adding fat in making croissants.

(i) Roll the dough into a rectangle about 8 mm thick. (ii) Cream 50 g butter or margarine and spread it over two-thirds of the length, leaving a 2 cm margin. (iii) Fold the unbuttered third over half of the buttered part and bring over the remaining part so that there are three layers of dough with two of fat. (iv) Seal the open edges with a rolling pin and roll again lightly so that the fat does not come out. (v) Repeat with the next two lots of 50 g fat and finally give a book fold.
Write the steps of preparing doughnuts.

(i) Prepare a soft yeast dough with flour, sugar, salt, eggs and milk and knead until smooth and elastic. (ii) Let it rise until double and knock back. (iii) Roll it to 1/2 inch and cut with a doughnut cutter. (iv) Prove the doughnuts on a floured duster until double. (v) Deep fry in new oil until golden brown on both sides, drain and roll in cinnamon sugar.
